Why We Have -- and Probably Will Keep Having -- Sluggish Job Growth

There's something that seems so evident, yet no economist seems to hit on. Productivity has skyrocketed and continues to grow. We can fundamentally break an economy down into production and the number of people required to maintain production. As productivity increases, the number of people required to maintain production drops. The technology enabling said gains does create new jobs, but the number it's creating in no way compare to the number that it takes away. And this problem exists independent of population. It's the ratio of workers per unit population to maintain production. It's why we see this pattern in tiny countries, small countries, huge countries, everywhere.

  • workforce participation figures (click on time to set the start date to before 2000)
  • productivity figures

Look at just about any of the dozens of countries listed there. You can almost perfectly predict a country's employment growth by simply looking at their productivity growth. Workforce productivity goes up -> employment goes down. And it's completely the opposite of what supply side economics, as this article is preaching, would predict. Increased productivity means more product produced per hour. That means more money. And that's supposed to mean more job growth and employment, but it doesn't.
